newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian cabinet to examine half a year of reform.
newsitem.headline: Russian cabinet to examine half a year of reform.

text.p: The Russian cabinet meets on Thursday to review its efforts in the first half of the year which have produced high hopes of growth despite some economic stumbling blocks still ahead.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin who has said the economy grew one percent in the first half is likely to give the main presentation, Interfax news agency said on Wednesday.
The exuberant prime minister has said the economy has turned round after years of stagnation.
An economy ministry forecast prepared for the meeting said gross domestic product would not rise this year and could decline up to two percent on last year's level, Interfax said.
Official figures say GDP contracted by 0.2 percent year-on-year in the first half of this year.
But sinking official forecasts, which began the year predicting growth, do not obscure optimism that Russia is finally making many of the hard choices real economic reform requires.
"Russia has made remarkable progress in stabilisation," European Union-funded Russian Economic Trends wrote in its second quarter report.
Taxmen have squeezed billions of dollars from delinquent payers such as natural gas monopoly Gazprom, bringing June receipts to targeted levels for the first time in months.
Officials have said they will restructure government debt to industry in the form of bonds payable in a few years and have promised to begin paying their current bills on time.

President Boris Yeltsin is making strong demands on the Treasury to pay some $2 billion in military and public sector wage arrears this year but appeared to back off from a less realistic plan of paying the wages by early autumn.

Direct foreign investment is still laughably low, measurable in a few billions of dollars per year, but Western investors are throwing money into stocks, pushing up the Russian Trading System index about 150 percent in the first half of the year.
Hard currency inflows have even threatened to disrupt Russia's clearest economic victory, control over inflation, as funds from investors desperate for Russian debt have broadened the money supply.

First Deputy Chairman Sergei Aleksashenko said the bank had sold Treasury bills from its portfolio in June and July to soak up funds from a successful Eurobond and a $700 million International Monetary Fund tranche.
"We have absorbed about $800 million," he said.

Chernomyrdin, who has weathered dozens of government changes in five years as prime minister, may also take some of the credit for reforms spearheaded by his younger colleagues, First Deputy Prime Ministers Boris Nemtsov and Anatoly Chubais.
Nemtsov brought a host of draft decrees and reformers on Wednesday to Yeltsin, vacationing in central Russia.

Yeltsin prohibited government guarantees on foreign credits for companies which are not paying taxes but gave the nod for Russia's largest company, electric company UES, to issue convertible bonds aimed at foreigners, Russian agencies said.
Five trillion roubles ($870 million) raised from the issue on government-owned shares will be used to pay off wage arrears, Nemtsov was quoted as telling the agencies.
